title: EIS Contribution Malaysia 2026: Rates, Table & Calculation
summary: EIS contribution Malaysia 2026: Explore PERKESO rates, the full contribution table, employer and employee deductions, and payment deadlines.
body_markdown:
A new joiner's first payslip has an EIS line that doesn't match what the payroll spreadsheet from last quarter said. It's a small discrepancy, but it's the kind that makes an HR manager stop and double-check everything else on the run.


Here's the short answer: EIS contribution in Malaysia is set at 0.4% of monthly wages, split 0.2% employer and 0.2% employee, capped once a salary crosses the RM6,000 wage ceiling. The rest of this guide covers the full table, who's actually covered, and how to calculate it correctly, so that discrepancy never happens again.


## What Is EIS Contribution?


The Employment Insurance System (EIS) is a mandatory contribution scheme administered by PERKESO (the Social Security Organisation) under the Employment Insurance System Act 2017, which came into force on 1 January 2018. It exists to give workers temporary financial support and re-employment help if they lose their job through no fault of their own, funded by monthly contributions from both employer and employee.


It's easy to confuse EIS with EPF and SOCSO since all three show up on the same payslip.


Scheme Purpose Employer Rate Employee Rate Wage Ceiling


EPF (KWSP) Retirement savings 12-13% 11% None


SOCSO (PERKESO) Workplace injury, invalidity ~1.75% ~0.5% RM6,000/month


EIS (SIP) Job loss protection 0.2% 0.2% RM6,000/month


**Note:** EIS and SOCSO are both run by PERKESO and submitted through the same portal, but they're legally separate schemes under different Acts, which is why they appear as two distinct line items on a payslip rather than one combined figure.


## EIS Contribution Rate and Table for 2026


The EIS contribution rate is 0.4% of an employee's monthly wages in total: 0.2% paid by the employer and 0.2% deducted from the employee's salary. The contribution wage ceiling is RM6,000 per month, meaning wages above that amount are still subject to EIS, but the deduction stops growing once it hits the ceiling rate.


PERKESO raised the contribution wage ceiling from RM5,000 to RM6,000 effective 1 October 2024, and it has stayed at RM6,000 through 2026. Before that, the ceiling moved from RM4,000 to RM5,000 in September 2022. Check the PERKESO website periodically rather than assuming the figure is permanent.


Pro Tip


Never calculate EIS by multiplying salary by 0.2% directly. PERKESO publishes a banded contribution table with fixed ringgit amounts for each wage range, and the table doesn't always match a straight percentage calculation at every band. Always look up the correct band.

## Who Must Contribute to EIS


Coverage looks broad on paper but has real edge cases that trip up payroll teams, especially around foreign hires and older employees.


Generally required to contribute:


- Malaysian citizens and permanent residents aged 18 to 60, employed under a contract of service or apprenticeship
- Full-time, part-time, temporary, and contract employees, as long as they meet the standard eligibility requirements
- Employees in the private sector, from the very first hire a company makes


Generally excluded:


- Foreign workers who are not Malaysian citizens or permanent residents (standard EIS coverage under Act 800 requires the employee to be a Malaysian citizen or permanent resident)
- Government employees and the self-employed
- Domestic workers, with a narrow exception: eligible local domestic workers who are Malaysian citizens or permanent residents can be covered, but foreign domestic workers are not
- Employees aged 57 and above who had no prior EIS contributions before turning 57


**Note:** Age 57 is a quiet edge case many payroll teams miss. An employee who joins a company for the first time at 58, with no contribution history before 57, is exempt from EIS entirely, even though they're still under the general 60-year cutoff.


Part-timers and contract staff are a common source of confusion, but the rule is simple: the classification that matters isn't the job title or hours worked. It's whether a contract of service exists. Registration isn't optional or delayed until a probation period ends. The moment a company hires its first eligible employee, it must register with PERKESO.


## How to Calculate EIS Contribution


The cleanest way to think about EIS is as a lookup, not a formula. Pull the employee's monthly wage, find their band on the PERKESO table, and read off both the employer and employee shares directly rather than running a percentage calculation by hand.


**Step 1: Identify EIS-liable wages.** EIS applies to an employee's monthly wages, which includes basic salary, fixed allowances, and overtime. Overtime is included within the definition of wages under the Employment Insurance System Act 2017, so it needs to be added to the base figure before looking up the band.


**Step 2: Find the correct wage band.** Match the total EIS-liable wage to its row in the PERKESO table. If the wage exceeds RM6,000, use the ceiling row rather than extrapolating further.


**Step 3: Read both shares and record them on the payslip.** Each band gives a fixed employer amount and employee amount in ringgit. Deduct the employee share from gross pay and add the employer share as a separate statutory cost, then record both on the payslip for audit purposes.


**Example 1 (below the ceiling):** An employee earns RM2,550 a month. That falls in the RM2,500.01 to RM2,600 band, so the employer pays RM5.10 and the employee pays RM5.10, for a combined RM10.20.


**Example 2 (above the ceiling):** An employee earns RM8,000 a month. Since this exceeds the RM6,000 ceiling, both employer and employee pay the maximum rate: RM11.90 each, RM23.80 combined, regardless of how much higher the actual salary is.


Pro Tip


If payroll software is calculating EIS as a flat 0.2% of salary instead of pulling from the banded table, double-check the output against a few sample salaries manually. A system built on the wrong assumption will be consistently off by small amounts that are easy to miss until an audit flags them.


## Payment Deadlines, Submission, and Penalties


EIS contributions are due alongside SOCSO, not as a separate payment. Employers do not need to make a separate transaction; both payments follow the same schedule and deadlines.


**Deadline:** Contributions must be paid no later than the 15th day of the immediately following month. Wages paid for January must have their EIS contribution settled by 15 February.


Submission channels:


- PERKESO ASSIST Portal
- Online banking
- Cheque, money order, or postal order
- Bank agents
- SOCSO counters


Penalties for late or missed payment:


Missing the deadline isn't a minor administrative slip. Late or missed contributions trigger interest, late-payment penalties, and potential prosecution under Section 75 of the Act, with directors personally liable. Reported interest on outstanding contributions is commonly cited around 6% per annum for each day of delay. Confirm the exact figure directly with PERKESO since penalty structures can be revised.


Beyond the monthly cycle, a few lifecycle events create their own obligations: registering every new eligible hire with PERKESO before their first payroll run, and reporting a loss of employment so the affected employee can file a claim within the 60-day window.


## Getting EIS Right in Your Monthly Payroll


Most EIS errors aren't dramatic. They're small, repeated mistakes that compound over a year of payroll runs.


The most common is a stale contribution table. PERKESO has revised the wage ceiling twice in under three years: from RM4,000 to RM5,000 in 2022 and from RM5,000 to RM6,000 in October 2024. A spreadsheet or payroll tool that wasn't updated after either change has been quietly under-deducting or over-deducting EIS for every employee near the old ceiling.


The second is miscounting wage components. Teams that exclude overtime or fixed allowances from the EIS-liable wage figure end up in the wrong band, sometimes for months, before anyone notices the discrepancy on an audit or a payslip query.


The third is missed new joiners. When onboarding and payroll run in separate systems, it's easy for a new hire's first pay cycle to go out without EIS registered at all, creating backdated contributions and interest charges that land weeks later.
